analysis.one_liner: Requires copy-protection technology in every digital media device by federal mandate.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced in March 2002 and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to set a mandatory copy-protection standard that every digital media device — computers, TVs, recorders, and software that handle copyrighted material — must include. Device makers, importers, and sellers could not ship equipment without it, and removing or altering the protection would carry civil penalties. The stated goal was to reassure movie, TV, and music companies that their works could not be pirated, so they would release more high-quality digital content and speed up broadband and digital TV adoption. If industry negotiations failed within a year, the FCC would write the rules itself.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners — the major motion picture studios, television programmers, and record labels — gain a federally backed lock on how their digital works can be copied and transmitted, enforced by an interstate commerce ban on nonconforming devices. The bill's findings argue this would also benefit consumers indirectly, by giving content owners the confidence to release more high-definition and online programming [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires that digital media devices — any hardware or software that reproduces, converts, or accesses copyrighted digital works — include and use government-approved standard security technologies, with the FCC adopting the standards by rule after a 12-month negotiation window among device makers, consumer groups, and copyright owners [S3].

Bans selling or transporting nonconforming digital media devices in interstate commerce, and prohibits knowingly removing or altering the standard security technology, with violations enforced under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act's remedies and statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per violation of the encoding rules [S3].

The bill's stated rationale is that secure protection of digital content is a precondition for content owners to release high-quality digital programming online and for over-the-air digital television, which the findings say will speed broadband adoption and the digital TV transition [S3].

Includes some consumer carve-outs: the encoding rules must account for fair use, and content owners may not use the standard technology to block a lawful recipient from making a personal in-home copy of an over-the-air broadcast, cable, or satellite program at the time it is performed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost in less flexible devices and software: every computer, recorder, and player that touches copyrighted material would have to obey a single government-approved copy-protection scheme, and circumventing or altering it would be a federal violation regardless of whether any copying was for personal use. Device manufacturers, importers, and sellers would bear compliance costs and liability, and internet services would have to preserve any attached security measures on content they store or transmit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates a single government-approved copy-protection system in essentially all consumer digital equipment, going far beyond targeting pirates — a person who knowingly removes or alters the security technology from a lawfully purchased device violates the Act, with statutory damages attached, even without proof of actual infringement [S3].

The consumer protections are narrow: the personal-copying carve-out covers only simultaneous in-home recording of broadcast, cable, and satellite programming, leaving the FCC's rulemaking — conducted with the Register of Copyrights — to define the rest of what users may do with purchased digital works [S3].

The standards negotiations among device makers and copyright owners would be exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, meaning the talks that produce the mandatory national standard would not be subject to the usual open-meeting and public-participation requirements [S3].

Critics would also note that restricting devices rather than infringers risks breaking legitimate uses — home networks, backup copies, archival and educational copying — and pushes innovation decisions from the market to a federal rulemaking process, a cost the bill's fair-use language acknowledges but does not fully resolve [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real but indirect benefits to consumers — more high-definition and online content if copyright owners' piracy fears were eased — while imposing direct, nationwide costs on how every consumer uses digital devices, backed by federal penalties. The protections for fair use and home copying were narrower than the restrictions were broad, and the closed-door process for setting the mandatory standard compounded the imbalance. On the whole, the restrictions on ordinary users' equipment outweighed the promised content benefits, which depended entirely on copyright owners voluntarily releasing more material.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the same day and sat there until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 without a committee vote, a floor debate, or any further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Ernest Hollings introduced the bill on March 21, 2002, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].

No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup, reported the bill, or scheduled floor consideration, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1] [S5].

The bill's sole sponsors were Sen. Hollings and five cosponsors — Sens. Stevens (R-AK), Inouye (D-HI), Breaux (D-LA), Nelson (D-FL), and Feinstein (D-CA) — four Democrats and one Republican out of 49 senators of each party [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept unrestricted use of their digital devices, and the consumer electronics and computer industries avoided a federal copy-protection mandate; the motion picture and recording industries, which had sought a government-enforced security standard, got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and four of five cosponsors were Democrats and one, Sen. Stevens of Alaska, was a Republican; no vote was ever taken, so no party split appears in the record.

industries.industry: Motion picture, television, and music industries
industries.note: The bill would hand copyright owners a federally mandated, government-enforced copy-protection system in every digital device, with a commerce ban and penalties backing it up. Their gain comes directly at the cost of consumers' flexibility in how they use media they have paid for.

Device makers would have to build the standard security technology into every product, bear compliance costs, and face liability for shipping nonconforming devices. Their interest in defeating the bill ran alongside consumers' interest in unrestricted devices.

industries.industry: Internet service providers and online services
industries.note: The bill requires interactive computer services to store and transmit with integrity any security measure attached to copyrighted material, adding operational burdens and legal exposure for carriers and platforms.
